topic: Social News Feed Ranking and Fanout

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's work through a social news feed, the kind where a user opens the app and sees posts from people they follow.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The central tension in this problem is always fan out on write versus fan out on read.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's define them clearly. Fan out on write means that when someone posts, we immediately insert a reference into every follower's feed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And fan out on read means we store the post once and assemble the feed at request time by querying everyone the viewer follows.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Fan out on write makes reads extremely fast, which matters because reads dominate by a huge factor in this product.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But the write amplification is brutal for accounts with millions of followers. One post becomes millions of inserts.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And most of those inserts are wasted, because only a small fraction of followers will open the app before the post is stale.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So the standard answer is a hybrid. Regular accounts fan out on write, and high follower accounts are merged in at read time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We set a threshold, maybe a hundred thousand followers, above which an account is flagged as a celebrity and excluded from push.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: At read time we take the precomputed feed, pull recent posts from the celebrities the viewer follows, and merge the two lists.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The merge is cheap because the celebrity set per viewer is small, usually a handful of accounts.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should cache the celebrity timelines aggressively, since millions of viewers pull the same few author timelines.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's define the data model. A post record holds the author, the content reference, the creation time and the visibility settings.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And the feed itself is a per user list of post identifiers with a ranking score, trimmed to some maximum length.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We do not store post content in the feed, only references, so an edit or deletion takes effect everywhere immediately.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Hydration happens at read time, fetching the actual post objects in a batch from the post store or cache.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That also lets us filter at read time. Blocked authors, deleted posts and changed privacy settings are all applied during hydration.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Without that, a deleted post would linger in millions of precomputed feeds and we would have to chase it down with deletes.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Now ranking. The simplest feed is reverse chronological, which is predictable and needs no machine learning.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: But engagement optimized feeds score each candidate on predicted interaction, then sort by that score instead of by time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The typical pipeline has three stages. Candidate generation, then a lightweight ranking pass, then a heavier model on the survivors.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Candidate generation might produce a few thousand posts, the light ranker cuts that to a few hundred, and the heavy ranker orders the final page.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That staged funnel is what keeps latency acceptable, because the expensive model only ever sees a small candidate set.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Features would include the viewer's past interaction with the author, recency, content type and early engagement signals on the post.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should also apply diversity rules after ranking, so the feed does not show ten consecutive posts from the same author.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And integrity filters, removing content that violates policy or that the viewer has explicitly muted.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's talk about the serving path latency. A feed request should complete in a couple hundred milliseconds at the ninety ninth percentile.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That means the precomputed feed lookup must be a single cache read, and hydration must be one batched multi get.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Pagination needs a stable cursor, because if we paginate by offset the list shifts under the user as new posts arrive.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: A cursor encoding the last seen position and the ranking snapshot avoids duplicates and gaps when scrolling.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For the write path, posting should be fast for the author. We persist the post, acknowledge, then fan out asynchronously.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The fan out worker reads the follower list and writes into feed stores in batches, with backpressure so a spike does not overwhelm the cluster.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should prioritize active followers first, so people likely to open the app soon get the post before dormant accounts.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That is a nice optimization. It cuts the perceived fan out latency dramatically even if the full fan out takes minutes.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: In fact for dormant users we could skip the push entirely and rebuild their feed on read when they eventually return.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That saves an enormous amount of write volume, since a large fraction of registered accounts are inactive on any given day.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Storage wise, feeds are pure cache. We can always rebuild them from the posts and the follow graph if we lose them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So we can keep them in memory with a bounded length, say the most recent few hundred entries, and rebuild on a miss.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The follow graph itself needs to be fast to traverse, since fan out and read time assembly both depend on it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We store followers and following as separate adjacency lists, because the two directions are queried in different code paths.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: For very large follower lists we paginate the traversal, and the fan out job processes them in chunks rather than loading them all.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's cover the cold start case. A brand new user follows nobody, so their feed is empty.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We fill it with popular and topical content based on declared interests, and gradually shift to graph based content as they follow accounts.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For observability, we should track feed latency, cache hit ratio, fan out lag and the fraction of the feed that comes from the read path merge.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Fan out lag is the key health metric. If it grows, users see stale feeds even though nothing is technically broken.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should alert on that lag rather than on worker queue depth, because lag directly maps to user experience.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: To summarize, hybrid fan out with a celebrity threshold, reference only feed storage with read time hydration and filtering.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Plus a staged ranking funnel, cursor based pagination, activity prioritized fan out and feeds treated as rebuildable cache.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The elegant part is that the feed is disposable. Everything can be reconstructed, which makes the operational story much easier.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Agreed. Treating the derived data as cache rather than as a source of truth removes an entire class of consistency problems.
